title: The Enlightenment & Modern Politics
hook: The radical idea that legitimate power comes from the people — not God or birth — was forged in the Enlightenment, and it still underpins democracy today.
key_points: The Enlightenment (17th–18th c.) prized reason, individual rights, and questioning inherited authority.
Thinkers argued government should rest on the consent of the governed, not divine or hereditary right.
It produced ideas of natural rights, the social contract, and separation of powers.
These ideas directly inspired modern constitutions and democratic revolutions.
content_html: If ancient Greece and Rome supplied the vocabulary of self-rule, the Enlightenment supplied the modern argument for it. Spanning roughly the 17th and 18th centuries, this intellectual movement made reason, evidence, and individual rights its watchwords and turned a skeptical eye on inherited authority of every kind — the church, the aristocracy, and above all the claim that monarchs ruled by divine right. The question Enlightenment thinkers pressed was disarmingly simple and deeply subversive: by what right does anyone rule over anyone else?
extra_html: Their answers reshaped politics. Rejecting divine and hereditary right, they argued that legitimate authority must rest on the consent of the governed. From this came a cluster of now-familiar ideas: that individuals possess natural rights that no government may justly violate; that government originates in a social contract among the people and can be reformed or replaced if it breaks that trust; and that power should be separated into distinct branches so it cannot be abused. Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the Enlightenment as the era in which these principles were systematically developed and popularized. Their consequences were concrete: the period's ideas fed directly into the great democratic revolutions and the written constitutions and bills of rights that followed, embedding "consent of the governed" and protected rights into the design of modern states. The democratic order much of the world now takes for granted is, in large part, the Enlightenment's argument made into institutions.

related.title: The Social Contract
related.hook: Why should anyone obey the state? The social contract answers: people trade some freedom for the security and order that only collective authority can provide.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

related.title: Key Political Thinkers
related.hook: A handful of thinkers, writing across two millennia, still frame the questions we argue about: who should rule, why obey, and how to stop power going bad?

flashcards.prompt: What was the Enlightenment's radical claim about political power?
flashcards.back_html: That legitimate authority comes from the consent of the governed — not from divine right or birth — and should be guided by reason.

flashcards.prompt: Which ideas central to modern democracy were developed in the Enlightenment?

choices.text: Natural rights, the social contract, and separation of powers

flashcards.explanation_html: Enlightenment thinkers articulated natural rights, government by consent, and dividing power — foundations of modern constitutions.
